what_it_does: In large data centers, a surprising fraction of memory traffic — data moving between processors and RAM — is completely useless. Two specific cases stand out: data written back to RAM from a processor's on-chip cache after the memory it occupied has already been freed by the program (so the write carries no meaningful information), and data fetched from RAM that a program allocated but never initialized with real content (so the read brings in garbage). Necro-reaper eliminates this dead traffic by adding new CPU instructions that let software tell the hardware when a memory region has been freed or is uninitialized, so the hardware can simply skip the corresponding memory operations. A profiling-guided compiler identifies short-lived heap allocations at compile time and inserts these new instructions automatically; a customized memory allocator extends the annotations to cover the deallocation moment. The approach takes advantage of the fact that large data centers often control the entire software and hardware stack together, making it practical to change multiple layers simultaneously.
